title: Apostles too may have written pious letters beneath canonical authority — 1 Cor. 5
source_text: VIII. Similiter Apostoli nostri, praeter eas Epistolas, quae Canonicam authoritatem in Ecclesia habere meruerunt, multas alias potuerunt scribere, pias quidem & sanctas, attamen non ejusdem cum prioribus illis authoritatis, ut quae a Deo non fuerunt inspiratae, sicut illae, immediate, & extraordinarie. Talis potuit esse Epistola illa Pauli cujus mentio fieri videtur 1 Corinth. 5. ubi sic ait Apostolus, Scripsi vobis in epistola ne commisceamini cum scortatoribus. Ista enim videntur commode referri non posse nisi ad aliam quandam ad Corinthios epistolam, quae priorem illam praecesserit. Quanquam sunt multi viri docti, tam ex nostris, quam ex Pontificiis, qui nolunt ibi Paulum designare epistolam quandam quae fuerit ab illa ipsa quam tunc scribebat diversa. Sed verba ejus sic interpretantur, scripsi vobis in hac epistola: Ut Paulus non respiciat ad aliam quandam epistolam, sed ad illa ipsa quae superius scripserat, de repurgando fermento, & e medio ipsorum tollendo illo scortatore, qui uxorem patris habebat.
pass_a_gloss: Likewise our Apostles, besides those Epistles which deserved to have Canonical authority in the Church, could have written many others, pious indeed and holy, yet not of the same authority as those former ones, as not inspired by God immediately and extraordinarily as those were. Such could have been that Epistle of Paul of which mention seems to be made in 1 Corinthians 5, where the Apostle says, I wrote to you in an epistle not to company with fornicators. For those words seem unable conveniently to be referred except to some other epistle to the Corinthians which preceded that former one. Although there are many learned men, both of ours and of the Pontiffs, who do not want Paul there to designate some epistle different from the very one he was then writing. But they interpret his words thus: I wrote to you in this epistle — so that Paul does not look back to some other epistle, but to those very things he had written above about purging out the leaven and removing from their midst that fornicator who had his father's wife.
pass_b_english: Apostles could write other pious letters that never rose to canonical, immediately inspired authority.
1 Cor. 5 may point to an earlier Corinthian letter — if so, a holy but non-canonical piece, not a lost rule of faith.
Many Reformed and Roman scholars instead read 'in this epistle,' pointing back to Paul's words already in the same letter about the incestuous man.
Either way, Rome gains no vanished second Canon equal to Scripture.
